Why Managed Infrastructure

The cloud still runs on physical servers that somebody must operate

Cloud Service Models

Moving right transfers more infrastructure operations to the provider

Serverless ComputingServerless transfers server provisioning and operation to a managed service

The service scales servers behind the application interface

Milestones in Managed Analytics

Analytics shifted from operating clusters to submitting SQL to a service

BigQuery as a Managed Service

Analysts submit SQL while the service manages distributed execution

Spark and BigQuery

ToolUser expressesTypical responsibility
SparkA distributed programChoose transformations and execution environment
Managed Spark serviceA Spark programUse a provider-managed execution environment
BigQueryAn analytical SQL queryDefine tables and the analytical question

Why an Analytical Warehouse

Shared analytical tables connect multiple sources to consistent departmental reports

OLTP and OLAPOnline Transaction Processing (OLTP) and Online Analytical Processing (OLAP)

Small transactional updates and large analytical scans place different demands on storage

Workloads Shape Physical Storage

WorkloadRead / write patternTypical physical choice
OLTPFind and update a few complete recordsRow store + key indexes
OLAPScan a few columns across many recordsColumn store + compressed scans
Mixed workloadFresh writes and large analytical readsSeparate replicas or a hybrid design
OLTP favors record access; OLAP favors scanning selected attributes

The Same Values on Disk

Logical table

CountryProductSales
IndiaChocolate1000
IndiaIce-cream2000
GermanyChocolate4000
USNoodle500

Row store

Column store

Twelve values retain their meaning while their physical order changes

Point Reads and Analytical Scans

Choose a layout around the values that the workload needs to read

The Tradeoff Is Read and Write Amplification

OperationRow layoutColumn layout
Read one full recordFetch nearby attributesGather values across column segments
Scan 3 of 100 columnsRead unwanted attributes in scanned pagesRead the selected column segments
Frequent record updatesUpdate record and its indexesMaintain deltas or rewrite compressed segments
The preferred layout depends on how much data each operation must touch

Columns Enable Compact Encoding

EncodingOne product columnEncoded representation
DictionaryChocolate, Ice-cream, Chocolate, Chocolate0, 1, 0, 0 + dictionary
Run-length0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 0(0,3), (1,2), (0,1)
SELECT SUM(amount)
FROM sales WHERE product = 'Chocolate';
Repeated values and shared types enable encodings that reduce scan input

Prune Columns and Partitions

SELECT product_id, SUM(amount)
FROM sales
WHERE sale_date >= DATE '2025-10-01'
  AND sale_date <  DATE '2025-11-01'
GROUP BY product_id;
ProjectionPartition filterRemaining work
product_id, amount, sale_dateOctober partitions onlyScan, group and combine selected data
Column selection and partition pruning remove different parts of the scan

Inside BigQueryHistorical architecture: follow the query and its data

SQL execution, columnar storage and the network form separate service layers

BigQuery Storage and Compute

Persistent table storage and query execution are managed as separate layers

Managed Fault ToleranceHistorical illustration of replicated storage

Replicated storage protects against infrastructure failures rather than incorrect analytical logic

Distributed Query Execution

Workers read portions of the table and combine partial results

Partial Results Must Be Mergeable

SELECT country, COUNT(*)
FROM sales GROUP BY country;
WorkerPartial countsRoot merge
AIndia: 2, US: 1India: 2 + 1 = 3
BIndia: 1, US: 3US: 1 + 3 = 4
Local COUNT results become a global SUM over the same group key

Averages Need Sums and Counts

WorkerValuesPartial state
A10, 10sum = 20, count = 2
B90sum = 90, count = 1
AVG = (20 + 90) / (2 + 1) = 36.67
(10 + 90) / 2 = 50    -- wrong: unequal group sizes
An aggregate is distributed by preserving the state needed for a correct merge

Why Keep a Data Lake

Source files can remain in object storage before analytical tables are defined

ETL and ELTExtract, Transform, Load (ETL) or Extract, Load, Transform (ELT)

Transform before loading, or load detail first and transform inside the warehouse

Choosing ETL or ELTPlace transformation where data controls and processing resources require it

DecisionETL: transform before loadingELT: load before transforming
Data boundaryRemove identifiers before shared analyticsKeep raw input in a restricted landing area
Compute locationUse upstream compute; reduce target loadUse scalable warehouse SQL compute
Changing analysisLoad a known, validated target shapeRetain detail; rebuild models as needs change
Choose by data boundaries, available compute and the need to reprocess

From Lake to Warehouse

Separate raw and analytical stores introduce copying, transformations and refresh dependencies

Why a Lakehouse

Lakehouse adds table management over lake files for shared analytical use

What Makes a Lakehouse Work

LayerMechanismReason
Table managementTransactions and versioned metadataReaders see a consistent table
Query executionColumnar files, pruning and statisticsSQL scans avoid unrelated data
Shared accessSQL and DS/ML use the same snapshotFewer independent data copies
Table transactions, query execution and shared data access turn files into managed tables

Commit a Table Snapshot

An atomic metadata commit publishes a complete file set to readers

Tools Around a Lakehouse

Storage, file format, table format and compute belong to different layers

Why Data Orchestration

A successful query can still run before its required data is ready

Airflow at Airbnb

Airflow grew from a company workflow tool into an Apache project

Case study: Airbnb Experiment AnalyticsHistorical Airbnb workflow: configuration, computation and experiment metrics

Experiment configuration drives a dependency graph that produces analytical results

A Sales Workflow DAGA Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) defines tasks and their dependencies

Sales and products can load independently; the join waits for both inputs

Read a Real Dependency GraphHistorical Airflow maintenance DAG

Independent branches can progress while descendants of a failed task remain blocked

Tasks, Operators and Sensors

ConceptMeaningSales workflow example
TaskOne defined unit of workLoad the sales file
OperatorA template used to create a taskSubmit a SQL query
SensorA waiting task patternWait for the input file
A workflow combines concrete tasks built from reusable execution and waiting patterns

Define the Run PolicyAirflow 2.10 example: policy inside the DAG definition

from airflow import DAG
import pendulum
from datetime import timedelta

with DAG("daily_sales",
    start_date=pendulum.datetime(2025, 10, 2, tz="UTC"),
    schedule="@daily", catchup=False,
    default_args={"retries": 2,
                  "retry_delay": timedelta(minutes=5)}) as dag:
    ...
A schedule creates run instances; retries apply to tasks within each run

Wait for Complete Input, Then Run SQLAirflow 2.10 + common-sql 1.26; connections and SQL file configured separately

from airflow.sensors.filesystem import FileSensor
from airflow.providers.common.sql.operators.sql import SQLExecuteQueryOperator

# Inside the DAG context from the previous slide
wait = FileSensor(task_id="wait_for_sales",
    filepath="sales/{{ data_interval_start | ds }}/_SUCCESS",
    fs_conn_id="sales_files", mode="reschedule", timeout=3600)
load = SQLExecuteQueryOperator(task_id="load_daily",
    conn_id="warehouse", sql="load_daily.sql")
wait >> load
A sensor checks readiness; the downstream operator submits the transformation

Airflow Control and WorkersHistorical architecture: focus on the responsibilities, rather than deployment details

Scheduling, task execution and recorded state are distinct responsibilities

An Airflow RunApache Airflow interface

A real run shows succeeded, failed and waiting tasks

Caveat: An Upstream Failure

A failed product load prevents the dependent join from using incomplete inputs

Read Execution Time in GanttHistorical Airflow Gantt: actual overlap and long-running tasks

Use task durations together with dependencies to locate the path delaying completion

Data Interval and Run Time

The date being recomputed can differ from the time when the task runs

Catchup, Backfill and Retry

MechanismUnit of workWhat stays fixed
Retry / clear taskA task instance in an existing runIts data interval
CatchupMissing scheduled intervalsThe DAG timetable
BackfillSelected historical intervalsThe transformation applied to each interval
Re-execution changes when work runs, rather than which data interval it should read

Answer: Repeatable Date Load

BEGIN;
DELETE FROM daily_sales WHERE sale_date='2025-10-03';
INSERT INTO daily_sales
SELECT sale_date,SUM(amount) FROM fact_sales
WHERE sale_date='2025-10-03' GROUP BY sale_date;
COMMIT;
-- run the same block again
SELECT * FROM daily_sales ORDER BY sale_date;
sale_datetotal
2025-10-02500
2025-10-03500
Idempotent load: rerunning the same date range leaves the same result

transform [failed]  ->  cleanup [success]
                       trigger_rule="all_done"
CheckWhat it actually establishes
Run statusTerminal states of leaf tasks
Task successThe task returned successfully
Data checks before publishRequired properties of the produced data
